result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.network_robustness()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Simulate progressive node removal and measure network degradation. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L34822-L34942){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.network_robustness( strategy="degree", steps=None, seed=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Network robustness](/assets/graphs/network-robustness.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The two diamonds sharing hub D, with filled badges giving the degree-based removal order: D first (degree 4), then B, C, E, F, A, G. The chart plots the largest component as a fraction of the 7 nodes after each removal: 1.0, then 0.43 once D is gone, falling to 0.29, 0.14, and 0." width="100%"} Removes nodes one at a time according to a strategy and records the fraction of nodes in the largest connected component at each step. Useful for studying essential genes and network vulnerability in protein–protein interaction networks. The removal order is fixed up front from the intact graph: nodes are ranked once by degree or betweenness (ties go to the lower node ID) or shuffled randomly, and are then removed in that order without re-ranking after each removal. After every removal the size of the largest connected component among the remaining nodes is divided by the *original* number of nodes. A curve that stays high means the network holds together; a curve that drops steeply after a few removals means the network depends on a handful of nodes. Common uses: - comparing targeted attacks (`"degree"`, `"betweenness"`) with random failure (`"random"`) to see whether a network relies on hubs - identifying networks, or parts of networks, that are fragile to the loss of key nodes - comparing the resilience of different networks of similar size Edge direction is ignored when measuring components (they are weakly connected components), and degree counts every incident edge. The graph itself is not modified; removal is simulated on a copy of its structure. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [strategy]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["degree"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Node removal strategy (the default is `"degree"`): - `"degree"`: remove highest-degree nodes first (targeted attack). - `"betweenness"`: remove highest-betweenness nodes first. Betweenness is computed once on the intact graph, which costs more than the degree ranking on large graphs. - `"random"`: remove nodes in random order. [steps]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of nodes to remove. The default, `None`, removes every node, so the curve ends at `(1.0, 0.0)`. Smaller values stop early, which is enough when you only care about the first few removals. Values larger than the node count behave like `None`. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed used to shuffle the removal order when `strategy="random"`. Pass an integer for a reproducible curve; the default, `None`, gives a different order on each call. It is ignored by the other strategies, which are deterministic. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return the robustness curve as a list of `(fraction_removed, largest_component_fraction)` tuples. If `False` (the default), return `self` for chaining. The curve is not written to the node or edge tables in that case, so use `return_dict=True` whenever you need the values. The call is still listed by `describe()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph | list[tuple[float, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The robustness curve (if `return_dict=True`) or `self`. The curve starts with `(0.0, f)`, where `f` is the largest-component fraction of the intact graph, and has one more point for each removed node, so it holds `steps + 1` tuples (or `node count + 1` with the default `steps=`). An empty graph gives `[(0.0, 0.0)]`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `strategy=` is not `"degree"`, `"betweenness"`, or `"random"`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two diamonds share the hub `D`, the only node of degree 4. A degree-based attack removes `D` first, which immediately splits the network into two three-node pieces: the largest component falls from `1.0` to `0.43` (3 of 7 nodes) after a single removal: ::: {#deec7979 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph() g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]) g.add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("D", "F"), ("E", "G"), ("F", "G"), ] ) curve = g.network_robustness(strategy="degree", return_dict=True) [(round(removed, 2), round(lcc, 2)) for removed, lcc in curve] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(0.0, 1.0), (0.14, 0.43), (0.29, 0.43), (0.43, 0.43), (0.57, 0.43), (0.71, 0.29), (0.86, 0.14), (1.0, 0.0)] ``` ::: ::: Random failure of the same number of nodes typically does far less damage early on. Here `steps=3` stops after three removals and `seed=` makes the order reproducible: ::: {#48ce9df7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} curve = g.network_robustness(strategy="random", steps=3, seed=1, return_dict=True) [(round(removed, 2), round(lcc, 2)) for removed, lcc in curve] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [(0.0, 1.0), (0.14, 0.86), (0.29, 0.71), (0.43, 0.43)] ``` ::: :::
